clue.text: A friend of 19 in Lincoln, New Zealand prayed for by 22 down 22

indicators.note: the friend's name is placed inside the president's nickname, as 'in Lincoln' says

parts.note: Abraham Lincoln, US president, was nicknamed Abe
in Bizet's opera of 19 across, Mercédès is one of the heroine's gypsy friends

explanation.surface: A friend of Carmen turns up in Lincoln and New Zealand, and a singer prays for her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' works on the president's nickname, not the city. The answer's opening A comes from that nickname, so the clue's first word 'A' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Janis Joplin's a cappella song asks the Lord to buy her this luxury German car, so it is literally prayed for.

clue.text: Take on appropriate accommodation for party

indicators.note: one word gives accommodation to another, holding it inside itself

parts.note: apt means appropriate or fitting
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A host takes on the job of finding suitable lodging for a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: To take on a child, policy or idea as one's own is to embrace it in this sense.

clue.text: Another court passage

parts.note: an extra one is another, an additional one

explanation.surface: A building has another passageway leading to a courtroom.
explanation.definitionFit: A short excerpt quoted from a book or document is a passage taken from it.

clue.text: Underground cell like this crossword, mostly

indicators.note: only most of the word is kept, its final couple of letters being dropped

parts.note: this Guardian puzzle is a cryptic crossword

explanation.surface: The setter likens an underground prison cell to the obscure puzzle being solved.
explanation.definitionFit: A vault beneath a church, often used for burial, is an underground chamber.

clue.text: One who's desperate kicks the bucket and swells

parts.note: Desperate Dan is the strongman cowboy of the British children's comic The Dandy
to kick the bucket is an idiom for dying

explanation.surface: A man at his wits' end dies and his body bloats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swells' looks like a verb about bloating but is the plural noun: swells are fashionable, smartly dressed men.
explanation.definitionFit: Swells, in old slang, are elegant men of fashion, synonymous with fops.

clue.text: With an evenly balanced disposition, starting to speak your mind as the UK went in 1965

indicators.note: only the opening letter of each of the three following words is used

parts.note: Britain's government announced in 1965 its switch to metric measures

explanation.surface: Someone even-tempered speaks their mind about Britain's change of measures in 1965.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposition' reads as temperament but means arrangement: something symmetric has its parts disposed evenly about an axis.
explanation.definitionFit: A shape whose halves mirror each other has a balanced arrangement of parts.

clue.text: See 1
Where might one find bubbles? In a half of bubbly — fancy that!

indicators.note: the shuffled word sits within the half word, as 'In' says
only the first three of the six letters are kept
fancy as a verb of imagination suggests the letters are reimagined in another order

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise at finding bubbles in half a glass of champagne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy that!' reads as an exclamation of surprise, but 'fancy' rearranges 'that' to ATHT, which goes 'In' the first half of 'bubbly'; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bubble bath foams up in the tub where a bather soaks.

clue.text: I don't mean to insult you: coffee non-negotiable

definitions.text: I don't mean to insult you

indicators.note: negotiable letters can be bargained into new positions; the printed word is split, its non joining the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone apologises for refusing to budge about coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'non-negotiable' looks like one word meaning fixed, but 'non' is fodder alongside 'coffee' and 'negotiable' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said as a polite apology before saying something that might offend.

clue.text: Epitome of elegance is certainly not turgid prose

definitions.text: Epitome of elegance is certainly not turgid prose

parts.words: Epitome of elegance is certainly not turgid prose
parts.note: the phrase for graceful movement is verse rather than prose, and moving rather than stagnant, so it is the opposite of turgid prose

explanation.surface: Something supremely graceful is contrasted with heavy, sluggish writing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone or something moving with flowing, effortless grace.

clue.text: See 8
Finally, who's got the whole world in his hands? Christ, ultimately

parts.words: who's got the whole world in his hands
parts.note: the Titan Atlas holds up the heavens, often pictured with the globe on his shoulders

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A hymn-like line about God holding the world, ending with an exclamation of Christ.
explanation.walkthrough: The gospel song 'He's Got the Whole World in His Hands' points to God, and 'Christ' looks like an exclamation; instead it is the Titan, plus the last letter of 'Christ'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean eventually, after a long wait.

clue.text: Ordered, fine and tidy spot

indicators.note: the letters are ordered, put into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A neat, tidy place is described as ordered, fine and tidy.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot someone in a crowd is to recognise and pick them out.

clue.text: Joins educational institution before setback

parts.note: uni is short for university
set, a collection, written backwards as the word's own 'back' says

explanation.surface: Someone enrols at a university before suffering a setback.
explanation.definitionFit: To join things is to bring them together into one, to combine them.

clue.text: Mostly gas-fired, this Latin period

indicators.note: most of the word is kept, dropping its final letter

parts.note: neon is a noble gas
something lit has been set on fire
hic is the Latin word for this

explanation.surface: A Latin text describes something largely gas-fired.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Stone Age is the prehistoric era when farming began, the final part of the Stone Age.

clue.text: No marinas need to be built in a landlocked country

indicators.note: the letters must be built into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A country with no coastline has no need to build marinas.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny republic is entirely enclosed by Italy, with no sea coast.

clue.text: Dance as Bedouin in his element?

parts.note: a desert dweller's element is the sand
the Bedouin are a nomadic Arab people

explanation.surface: A desert nomad dances as one perfectly in his element.
explanation.definitionFit: A stately Spanish court dance in triple time, later a movement in baroque suites.

clue.text: Not hotshot for a drop in temperature

parts.note: not hot means cold
a snap is a photograph, a shot

explanation.surface: Someone who is no hotshot is blamed for falling temperatures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hotshot' reads as one word, a star performer, but splits into 'Not hot' and 'shot'.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief spell of sudden cold weather is a fall in temperature.

clue.text: Start to draw lots for casual artwork

indicators.note: the start of the following word gives its first letter only

parts.note: oodles means lots, a great quantity

explanation.surface: People start to draw lots to decide who makes some informal art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw lots' reads as a phrase for picking by chance, but the words work separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Absent-minded scribbles made while thinking of something else are informal drawings.

clue.text: Map or schematic section driven by friends of 22 22 across

indicators.note: a section of the words is taken, the letters running across them

explanation.surface: A section of a map or diagram is driven over by a singer's friends.

clue.text: Opera for 6 across 18?

Karl Benz and Ferdinand Porsche were both ..., motor manufacturers

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words: Benz and Porsche are car men.

clue.text: Substitute crêpe filling with something dainty

parts.note: lace is a delicate, dainty fabric

clue.text: Creature is around, is around and is around no more?

explanation.surface: A riddle about a creature that keeps being around and then is not.
explanation.walkthrough: The closing 'and is around no more?' is a cryptic extra: these creatures are extinct.

New Year's Day's link includes place for musician

clue.text: Hotel computer equipment is common, is that not the case?

explanation.surface: Is hotel computer equipment ordinary, someone asks?

explanation.definitionFit: The slang tag question is a vulgar contraction meaning isn't it, used in casual British speech.
